strengths: Provides an elegant and unifying theoretical framework (RNE) that connects a wide range of previously disparate diffusion density-estimation and inference-time-control methods (Itô density estimator, Feynman-Kac density relation, FKC, TDS, FK-Steering) under a single Radon-Nikodym/time-reversal perspective, with rigorous derivations and explicit propositions showing when RNC reduces to FKC or TDS.

The identification and analysis of numerical instability in naive discretisation of the RN estimator, together with the proposed analytical-reference stabilisation and an accompanying convergence-rate proof (O(√Δt)), is a genuine and useful technical contribution beyond the conceptual unification.

Demonstrates flexibility by extending RNE/RNC to a broad set of practical settings: density estimation, annealing, model composition/product-of-experts, reward-tilting, and even discrete diffusion (CTMC), each backed by formal propositions.

Reasonably broad empirical validation spanning synthetic (GMM) density estimation, molecular simulation (ALDP, LJ-13) annealing, and real structure-based drug design tasks (multi-target ligand design, reward-tilted SBDD), with docking-score/QED/SA metrics and comparisons to strong recent baselines (FKC, TDS).

Extensive appendix with detailed proofs, ablations (RNDE-IS vs. reference, sensitivity to ca/cb), and implementation details, aiding reproducibility and giving good intuition for why/when the flexibility helps.
weaknesses: The core mathematical fact underlying the method (RN derivative between a process and its time-reversal is 1) is not new; the paper's contribution is primarily a unifying reformulation/relabeling of known results, and the incremental practical gain over FKC/TDS in experiments is often modest (e.g., ca=1,cb=0 essentially reproduces FKC).

The practical benefit of the framework's 'flexibility' hinges on tuning free hyperparameters (ca, cb, or general at/bt choices) per task via grid search, with no principled or automatic method proposed for selecting them; the paper itself notes the optimal balance is task-dependent, undermining the 'plug-and-play' framing.

Presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy (many overloaded symbols, forward/backward drifts, multiple R definitions), which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility for readers not already familiar with path-measure/Girsanov machinery, despite claims of simplicity.

Experimental sample sizes in the SBDD/molecular tasks are fairly small (e.g., 32 ligands per target, 15-20 targets), and improvements over baselines in Table 2/3 are sometimes within overlapping error bars, limiting the statistical strength of the empirical claims.

The reward-tilting drug design experiment shows only mild, somewhat inconsistent improvements (e.g., docking score fluctuates without clear trend), and the paper acknowledges diversity loss/mode collapse as a persistent unresolved limitation of the SMC-based approach.

Some claimed advantages (e.g., 'any bridge model' applicability, discrete diffusion extension) are stated somewhat briefly/deferred to appendix without full empirical demonstration in the main experiments.

strengths: The paper provides an elegant and intuitive unifying framework (RNE) that connects a number of previously disparate inference-time control and density-estimation methods (Itô density estimator, Feynman-Kac density relation, twisted diffusion sampler, Feynman-Kac corrector) through a single, simple principle: the Radon-Nikodym derivative between a diffusion and its time-reversal is identically one. The connections are made rigorous in the appendix with detailed derivations (Propositions 2.2, A.1, C.2-C.5).

The identification and analysis of the discretization instability of the naive Gaussian-kernel RNE estimator, together with the proposed analytical-reference fix, is a genuinely useful practical contribution, supported by both an intuitive explanation (Section 4) and a non-trivial convergence-rate proof (O(sqrt(Delta t)), Appendix A.4).

The framework is shown to generalize beyond the restrictive derivations of prior SMC correctors (FKC, TDS) by allowing flexible choices of sampling/target process drifts, and this added flexibility is empirically shown to improve effective sample size and downstream metrics (e.g., annealing TVD on ALDP, docking-score improvements in multi-target SBDD).

Reasonably broad experimental scope spanning toy density estimation (40-mode GMM), molecular dynamics systems (ALDP, LJ-13), and realistic structure-based drug design tasks (multi-target composition, reward-tilted generation), connecting theory to practically relevant applications.
Extension to discrete diffusion/CTMC settings (Appendix A.5) broadens the applicability of the framework beyond continuous-state diffusion models.
Clear mapping of related work in Figure 2 helps position the contribution relative to the existing literature.
weaknesses: The central mathematical fact underlying RNE (RND between a process and its time reversal equals one) is well known; the paper's novelty lies primarily in unification and repackaging of existing estimators as special cases, which, while valuable for clarity, is somewhat incremental relative to concurrent/prior work (Vargas et al. 2023, Skreta et al. 2024/2025, Karczewski et al. 2024, Wu et al. 2023) that the paper heavily builds on and cites as near-equivalent.

The claimed 'plug-and-play' and flexibility advantages are undercut by the need to hand-tune extra hyperparameters (e.g., c_a, c_b, lambda schedules) whose optimal values are shown to be task- and target-dependent (Section 2.3.3, Appendix B.2), with no principled or automated procedure for selecting them, limiting the practical plug-and-play claims.

Experimental validation, while broad in task types, is somewhat limited in scale and statistical rigor: small systems (22-atom ALDP, 13-particle LJ, 10D GMM), modest batch sizes, and only 15-20 protein-pocket pairs for the drug-design experiments; some tables (e.g., Table 1) lack variance/error bars, making it hard to assess significance of reported improvements over FKC/TDS baselines.

The reward-tilting results (Table 3) show inconsistent trade-offs (e.g., SA-reward reducing QED, QED+SA reward reducing docking score) that are explained post hoc and somewhat hand-wavily as stochasticity or diversity loss, without deeper analysis or mitigation.

SMC's intrinsic diversity/mode-collapse limitation is acknowledged but not meaningfully addressed; the paper's own analysis (Appendix B.2) shows that lower ESS can sometimes 'look better' on certain metrics merely due to collapse to a single mode, complicating interpretation of the reported gains.

The paper is dense and notation-heavy (many overloaded sub/superscripts on R, multiple process pairs across sections), which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility for readers not already familiar with the stochastic-process/time-reversal literature.

Comparisons are mostly limited to FKC/TDS and naive baselines (e.g., 'sum score', unguided annealing); broader comparisons to other inference-time control approaches (e.g., guidance-based methods, learned h-transform methods) are largely absent from the main quantitative results.

strengths: Presents a unifying theoretical framework (RNE) based on the Radon-Nikodym derivative between forward and time-reversed path measures, which cleanly connects and generalizes several existing density estimation and inference-time control methods (Ito density estimator, Feynman-Kac density relation, FKC, TDS, Feynman-Kac steering) under one intuitive lens.

The theoretical connections to prior work are rigorously proven (extensive appendix proofs showing FKC, TDS, and Ito estimator as special cases), lending strong technical credibility to the unifying claims.

The framework is genuinely flexible/plug-and-play: it allows arbitrary choices of sampling/target processes (not required to be exact time-reversals), which is shown to yield tunable performance gains (ca, cb sweep) over more rigid baselines like FKC and TDS.

Identifies and addresses a concrete practical issue (numerical instability of naive Gaussian-kernel RNE due to variance misalignment) with a principled fix (analytical reference process), backed by both empirical verification and a formal convergence-rate proof (O(sqrt(dt))).

Diverse and relevant experimental validation across density estimation (synthetic GMM), annealing (molecular systems ALDP, LJ-13), model composition/product (multi-target drug design), and reward-tilting (QED/SA optimization), with reasonable metrics (TVD, W2, docking scores) and comparisons to strong recent baselines (FKC, TDS).
Extends the framework to discrete diffusion (CTMC) in the appendix, broadening applicability.
Clear writing with good conceptual illustrations (Fig. 1, Fig. 2) that aid understanding of a fairly technical topic.
weaknesses: The gains over FKC/TDS in the main experiments are often modest or mixed (e.g., Table 2 SBDD results are close between RNC and FKC; Table 1 shows large gains only for specifically tuned (ca, cb) which requires task-specific tuning, undermining the 'plug-and-play' narrative to some extent).

The optimal choice of hyperparameters (ca, cb, or more general sampling/target process design) appears highly task- and even target-dependent (as acknowledged in Appendix B.2), and the paper does not provide clear practical guidance or an automated method for selecting these, which could limit real-world plug-and-play usability.
Density estimation experiments are limited to a single synthetic 10-D GMM benchmark; no evaluation on realistic high-dimensional data (e.g., images) is provided to demonstrate scalability of RNDE.

The SMC diversity/mode-collapse limitation is discussed but not deeply mitigated; the trade-off between ESS and sample quality is empirically illustrated but lacks a principled solution or adaptive scheme.

Some experimental sections (e.g., Table 3 reward-tilting) lack a comparison against other reward-guidance baselines (e.g., DPS, universal guidance, FKC/TDS variants for reward-tilting), making it harder to assess relative performance beyond internal ablations.

The theoretical stability analysis (Section 4, Appendix A.3-A.4) is fairly involved and somewhat disconnected from the main practical recommendations; it might benefit from a more concise takeaway or algorithmic guideline for practitioners.

strengths: Provides a genuinely unifying theoretical framework (RNE) connecting many disparate approaches in the literature (twisted diffusion sampler, Feynman-Kac corrector/steering, Ito density estimator, Fokker-Planck regularisation, etc.), with careful, explicit derivations showing these are special cases of the proposed formalism (Appendix C.4, H.4).

Theoretically well-grounded, deriving RNE from the simple but powerful observation that the Radon-Nikodym derivative between a diffusion process and its time-reversal is identically one; this yields a flexible, plug-and-play recipe that generalizes across Gaussian diffusions, stochastic interpolants, bridges, and CTMCs (discrete diffusion).

Practical contribution beyond the abstract unification: identifies and fixes a concrete instability in naive discretization of RNE via an analytical reference process, with both empirical validation (Fig. 9, 10, 14) and a non-asymptotic convergence rate proof (Appendix G.3) showing O(sqrt(dt)) error, which is a nontrivial technical result.

Broad, diverse, and fairly rigorous experimental validation spanning molecular systems (ALDP, LJ-13), multi-target structure-based drug design, inference-time scaling, energy-based diffusion training (GMM up to 100D, ALDP), and downstream free-energy estimation via thermodynamic integration, with sensible baselines (FKC, TDS, dual score matching).

Good scientific transparency: the paper explicitly documents an erratum correcting an earlier incorrect claim about exact SMC weights for annealing/product cases, and includes a dedicated limitations section.

The macro-style, code-agnostic implementation design (Appendix A) is a meaningful practical advantage over FKC, which requires re-deriving weight formulas per task; the provided pseudocode supports reproducibility.

Extensive appendix ablations on ESS/variance trade-offs across multiple systems (ALDP, LJ-13, GMM) yield genuine scientific insight into when higher vs lower effective sample size is preferable depending on target modality.
weaknesses: The presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with many overloaded symbols (R, a/b/mu/nu processes, multiple path measure superscripts) that make the main text hard to follow without constantly cross-referencing the extensive appendix.

Some experimental comparisons show only marginal or mixed improvements over existing baselines (e.g., FKC) in Tables 1 and 3, and the gains attributed to flexibility (choice of ca, cb) rely on a hyperparameter sweep whose optimal setting appears task-dependent without a principled selection rule, somewhat undercutting the 'plug-and-play' simplicity claim.

The core theoretical device (Radon-Nikodym derivative between time-reversal path measures) and several specific applications were already established in prior work; the paper's novelty is primarily in unification, reference-process stabilization, and generalization to new settings rather than a fundamentally new estimator.

The perfect-diffusion-model assumption underlying the flexible RNC design (annealing, product, CFG) is explicitly noted as a limitation causing bias with imperfect models, but no empirical quantification of this bias is provided.

Some proofs (e.g., convergence rate proof in Appendix G.3) rely on fairly strong regularity/boundedness assumptions (Lipschitz drift, bounded moments, log-concavity of reference) that may not hold for all diffusion models used in practice, with limited discussion of practical implications.

The free-energy estimation experiment (Table 4) reports results from a single system (ALDP solvation) with limited statistical replication, making it hard to assess robustness of this downstream application claim.

strengths: Provides a genuinely useful unifying theoretical perspective (RNE) that connects a wide swath of previously disparate methods (FKC, TDS, Feynman-Kac steering, Ito density estimator, Fokker-Planck regularisation, etc.) under a single Radon-Nikodym derivative argument, with explicit proofs of equivalence/special-casing in the appendix.

The plug-and-play design is appealing: changing the task (anneal, reward-tilting, CFG/product) only requires swapping the sampling/target kernel functions without re-deriving weight formulas, unlike FKC which needs per-task derivations.
Extends beyond standard Gaussian diffusions to stochastic interpolants, bridge models, and CTMC/discrete diffusion, broadening applicability.

Identifies and addresses a real practical issue (numerical instability of naive Gaussian-kernel RNE) via an analytical reference process, with both intuitive explanation and a non-asymptotic convergence-rate proof (O(√Δt)).

Reasonably broad experimental suite: molecular annealing (ALDP, LJ-13), multi-target structure-based drug design, inference-time scaling, energy-based diffusion training (GMM, 100D GMM, ALDP as MLFF), and free-energy estimation via thermodynamic integration, with ablations on the (ca, cb) design space and reference process.
Transparent erratum correcting an earlier overclaim about exact SMC weights for annealing/product, which reflects positively on the authors' rigor even though it reveals a prior mistake.
weaknesses: Many of the claimed 'equivalences' to prior work (Ito density estimator, FKC special cases, Feynman-Kac density relation, Fokker-Planck regulariser) suggest the core estimator is not fundamentally new; the main contribution is largely a reframing/unification, and the degree of genuine methodological novelty beyond repackaging known RND arguments (e.g., Vargas et al. 2023b) is debatable.

Empirical gains over the closest baseline (FKC) are often modest (e.g., Table 3 SBDD results, Table 1 default ca=1,cb=0 matching FKC exactly) and depend on a task- and distribution-specific hyperparameter sweep (ca, cb) with no principled selection rule — the paper even admits the optimal choice is 'task-dependent' and trades off diversity vs. fidelity in an ad hoc way, undermining the 'plug-and-play' framing.

The practical instantiation requires several non-trivial design choices (analytical reference process, discretization scheme, hyperparameters ca/cb, λ_R for energy regularisation) that are tuned per experiment, raising reproducibility and generality concerns despite the 'flexible framework' narrative.

Several experiments are on small/toy or moderate-scale systems (2D/10D/100D GMMs, ALDP, LJ-13, 20 protein-pocket pairs with 32 ligands each) without large-scale image/video/language diffusion validation, limiting evidence that the benefits generalize to the large models where inference-time control is most impactful in practice.

The paper's notation and derivations are extremely dense (many propositions deferred to a ~30-page appendix), which could hinder independent verification and practical adoption despite the 'macro-style' plug-and-play claim.

The erratum indicates that a previous version contained an incorrect theoretical claim about exact SMC weights for annealing/product settings, raising some concern about the care taken in deriving other theoretical results in the current version.

strengths: Provides a genuinely unifying theoretical framework (RNE) connecting many previously disparate approaches for diffusion density estimation, inference-time control (SMC weight computation), and energy-based diffusion training, all derived from the simple but powerful observation that the Radon-Nikodym derivative between a diffusion process and its time-reversal is identically 1.

Rigorously demonstrates that several existing methods (twisted diffusion sampler, Feynman-Kac corrector, Feynman-Kac steering, Ito density estimator, Feynman-Kac density estimator, Fokker-Planck regularizer) are special cases of RNE, with detailed proofs in the appendix (Appendix C.4, D, H.4) showing exact correspondences under specific hyperparameter choices.

The plug-and-play macro-style algorithm design (Appendix A pseudocode) is a meaningful practical contribution: users can freely swap sampling/target process choices without re-deriving importance weight formulas for each new task, unlike FKC which requires per-task derivation.

Identifies and fixes a genuine practical instability issue (variance misalignment in discretized forward/backward kernels) via the analytical reference process, with both theoretical convergence-rate analysis (Proposition G.1, showing O(√Δt) convergence) and empirical validation.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation across multiple domains and modalities: molecular systems (ALDP, LJ-13), GMM, structure-based drug design (multi-target SBDD with real docking scores), energy-based diffusion training, and free-energy estimation via thermodynamic integration — showing consistent, often substantial improvements over strong baselines (FKC, TDS, DSM, dual score matching).

The paper is unusually thorough and transparent about limitations, including an explicit erratum correcting an error from a previous version regarding the reward-tilting weight formula's inapplicability to annealing/product cases — this kind of self-correction increases trust in the work's rigor.

Extends the framework beyond continuous Gaussian diffusions to CTMCs (discrete diffusion) and stochastic interpolants/bridge models, demonstrating genuine generality rather than a narrow Gaussian-diffusion-specific trick.

Practical significance is well-supported: negligible computational overhead is repeatedly emphasized and empirically shown (e.g., energy regularization improves free energy TI estimates from 27.30±0.45 to 29.28±0.04 against reference 29.43±0.01).
weaknesses: The core mathematical fact underlying RNE (RND between a process and its time-reversal is 1) is a known/classical identity; the primary novelty lies in the systematic application and unification rather than a fundamentally new theoretical result, so the conceptual leap, while valuable, is somewhat incremental relative to concurrent works like Karczewski et al. 2024 and Skreta et al. 2024, which the paper itself acknowledges are theoretically equivalent for the density estimation case.

The flexibility touted for RNC (arbitrary choice of sampling/target processes at, bt) comes with no principled guidance on how to choose these in general beyond heuristics and a coefficient sweep (ca, cb); the paper's own analysis (Appendix F.3) shows the optimal choice is highly task/target dependent (unimodal vs multimodal), which somewhat undercuts the 'plug-and-play' simplicity claim for practitioners without extensive tuning.

Non-asymptotic convergence guarantees (Section G.3) are only provided for the case of linear drift µt with Gaussian reference process, and the authors explicitly state that a rigorous non-asymptotic analysis of RNE without the reference process is left to future work, leaving a gap in theoretical completeness.

Reliance on the perfect-diffusion-model assumption for the annealing/product/CFG SMC weight derivations (as opposed to reward-tilting, which has an exact correction under model imperfection) means bias from model imperfection is not fully addressed for several of the paper's main use cases, a limitation acknowledged but not resolved.

Some empirical comparisons (e.g., Table 1 ALDP annealing, Table 3 SBDD) show gains over FKC that are real but sometimes modest in absolute terms (e.g., product experiment improvements in 'better than known' metric), and the improvements depend on hyperparameter sweeps (ca, cb) that were tuned on the same evaluation metrics being reported, raising some concern about overfitting to the test criteria versus genuine generalizable gains.

The paper is extremely dense with many propositions, corollaries, and appendix cross-references, which may reduce accessibility and reproducibility for readers who are not already familiar with path-measure/Girsanov-theorem-style derivations; some core practical takeaways are somewhat buried in the appendix.
